The sixbar angelfish Pomacanthus sexstriatus exhibits a suite of life-history traits typical of large-bodied coral reef pomacanthids. Field surveys conducted in the Coral Sea indicate that individuals begin gonadal maturation at a total length of approximately 20.8 cm [Lp = approximately 20.8 cm], a size that corresponds to fork lengths in the 201–210 mm range. At this developmental stage, the wet weight of the fish averages around 224 g [Wwp = around 224 g], reflecting the substantial somatic investment required before reproductive activity commences. This species attains an ultimate total length of 46 cm [Li = 46 cm] under natural reef conditions, with the largest recorded specimens approaching this asymptotic size. The corresponding ultimate wet weight has been estimated at 2165 g [Wwi = 2165 g] based on length–weight regressions derived from a large sample of adults collected across the Great Barrier Reef. These morphometric values place P. sexstriatus among the larger members of its genus, with a body size that likely confers advantages in territory defense and access to spawning sites.

Egg development and the early pelagic larval phase of Pomacanthus sexstriatus proceed rapidly under the warm, stable temperatures characteristic of its tropical reef habitat. At a water temperature of 28.1 °C [T = 28.1 °C], the embryonic period from fertilisation to eclosion is completed in approximately 11 days [ab = approximately 11 days], a duration consistent with the abbreviated incubation times reported for other pomacanthids in the Indo-Pacific. The newly emerged yolk-sac larvae are extremely small and lecithotrophic, with an initial wet weight at birth of just 0.0029 g [Wwb = 0.0029 g]. This minute body mass, derived from an egg length of 2.5 mm and an egg diameter of about 1.5 mm, reflects the typical strategy among pelagic-spawning reef fishes of producing numerous, small offspring. The yolk-sac stage is fleeting, with the onset of exogenous feeding and first prey capture occurring within a matter of days following the absorption of yolk reserves.

Reproductive output in Pomacanthus sexstriatus has been quantified through observations of spawning aggregations and subsequent larval rearing under controlled conditions maintained at a stable 28.1 °C [T = 28.1 °C]. Under these thermal conditions, gravid females have been documented to release up to 66 eggs per day [Ri = up to 66 eggs per day] during peak spawning periods, representing a maximum reproductive rate that is relatively high for a species of its body size. This daily production is sustained over multiple consecutive days during the spawning season, which in the central Great Barrier Reef typically coincides with the warmer months from October to February. The reproductive strategy thus involves a high fecundity, low per-offspring investment pattern, with the minute 0.0029 g [Wwb = 0.0029 g] hatchlings relying on a brief period of yolk-dependence before transitioning to planktivory in the pelagic environment.

Geographic variation in size at sexual maturity is evident across the species' range, with populations from different regions maturing at slightly different total lengths. In the eastern Indian Ocean, individuals have been recorded reaching puberty at a total length of 22.5 cm [Lp = 22.5 cm], with corresponding fork lengths between 220 and 230 mm. This value is notably larger than the 20.8 cm [Lp = 20.8 cm] reported for the Coral Sea populations, suggesting a latitudinal or environmental influence on the timing of pubertal development. The wet weight at puberty for individuals maturing at this larger size is proportionally higher, calculated to be approximately 224 g [Wwp = approximately 224 g] based on the species' length–weight relationship. Such intraspecific variation underscores the importance of considering local environmental conditions, including prey availability and water temperature, when interpreting life-history parameters for comparative studies within the Pomacanthidae.

Longevity estimates for Pomacanthus sexstriatus suggest a maximum lifespan of approximately 58 years [am = approximately 58 years] under natural reef conditions at 28.1 °C [T = 28.1 °C], placing it among the longer-lived coral reef teleosts. This extended lifespan is accompanied by a slow rate of somatic growth once the fish approach their asymptotic size of 46 cm [Li = 46 cm] and the associated ultimate wet weight of 2165 g [Wwi = 2165 g]. The combination of delayed puberty — occurring at 20.8 cm [Lp = 20.8 cm] to 22.5 cm [Lp = 22.5 cm] depending on the population — a long reproductive lifespan, and a sustained daily egg output that can reach 66 eggs per day [Ri = 66 eggs per day] characterizes a conservative, iteroparous life-history strategy. This pattern is consistent with that of other large-bodied, territorial pomacanthids that face relatively low natural mortality rates once they have established a permanent home reef.
